sections.title: A sideways face on a noticeboard
sections.intro_md:
On 19 September 1982, at 11:44 in the morning, a computer scientist at Carnegie Mellon University typed three characters into the department's online noticeboard: **:-)**. A joke about a mercury spill in a lift had been taken seriously, a safety warning had followed, and Scott Fahlman suggested a fix. Mark the jokes, so nobody has to guess.

Nobody voted on it. No company shipped it. Within months the sideways face had spread to other universities over the ARPANET, and within a decade it was everywhere text was typed. That is the paradox of internet culture. It has no capital, no king and no rulebook, yet millions of strangers end up sharing the same jokes, words, manners and taboos, often within days.

Today is about how that happens. Internet culture is the shared behaviour, language, humour, values and artefacts of people who meet through networks. It forms the way any culture forms, by imitation and belonging, only faster, louder and with every step written down.

spotlights.name: The first smiley, Carnegie Mellon, 1982
spotlights.spot_it: A colon, a hyphen and a closing bracket, read with your head tilted left. The original post signs off 'Scott E Fahlman'.
spotlights.story_md: The thread began with a physics puzzle: what happens to a drop of mercury in a lift when the cable snaps? Someone joked that the lift was contaminated, and some readers believed it. Fahlman proposed **:-)** for jokes and **:-(** for things that are not. The post itself was lost for twenty years, until Jeff Baird recovered it from old backup tapes in September 2002. Fahlman never made money from it, and he has said he prefers the plain typed version to the graphical smileys that followed. What he spotted was the core problem of text online: it strips away the face and tone that tell us how to read a sentence. Every later emoticon, emoji and 'lol' is a repair for that loss.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the first documented case of an online community inventing a convention to fix a problem that only text conversation has.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tilt your head: the internet's first social rule was a face lying on its side.

spotlights.name: Godwin's law
spotlights.spot_it: Any time someone online says 'and that is how Godwin's law ends this thread', or says a Nazi comparison means the argument is over.
spotlights.story_md: In 1990 the lawyer Mike Godwin noticed that Usenet arguments kept sliding into comparisons with Hitler, which made the comparisons meaningless. He wrote a rule: as an online discussion grows longer, the probability of a comparison involving Nazis or Hitler approaches one. Then he spread it on purpose, posting it wherever the comparison appeared. In WIRED in 1994 he called it a deliberate **counter-meme**, an idea released to change behaviour. It worked well enough that many forums treated the first Nazi comparison as an automatic loss. Godwin himself has said the law was never meant to ban all such comparisons, and in 2017 he wrote that comparing marchers in Charlottesville to Nazis was fair.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that a norm can be engineered by one person and still be adopted by millions as if it had always existed.
spotlights.memory_hook: One lawyer wrote a joke rule, and the internet started obeying it.

sections.title: What internet culture actually is
sections.intro_md:
Culture, in the anthropologist's sense, is everything a group learns rather than inherits: its language, jokes, manners, beliefs and objects. **Internet culture** is that, among people who meet through networks. It includes the obvious things, memes, slang and emoji, and the less obvious: the habit of lurking before posting, the expectation that you search before asking, the belief that information should be free, and the instinct to answer outrage with irony.

There is no single internet culture. There are thousands of overlapping ones, from a Wikipedia talk page to a gaming Discord to an aunties' WhatsApp group. What they share is a set of forces: anyone can publish, everything can be copied and changed, and everything is recorded.

The scale is now planetary. In 2025 the International Telecommunication Union estimated that **6 billion people** were online, about three quarters of humanity, with **2.2 billion** still offline. India alone had about **958 million** active users, according to IAMAI and Kantar. The three ideas below are the toolkit scholars use to make sense of all this.

spotlights.name: Dawkins coins 'meme'
spotlights.spot_it: The word meme, rhyming with cream, in chapter 11 of a book about genes: 'Memes: the new replicators'.
spotlights.story_md: In **The Selfish Gene** (1976), the biologist Richard Dawkins needed a name for a unit of culture that copies itself from mind to mind the way a gene copies itself from body to body. He shortened the Greek **mimeme**, 'something imitated', to make it sound like gene. His examples were tunes, catchphrases, clothes fashions and ways of making pots. A meme survives if it is easy to copy, copied faithfully and copied often. Decades later the internet took the word for captioned pictures. Dawkins said in 2013 that the internet meme was a hijacking of his idea, then added that the hijacking fitted the original idea well: the word itself had mutated and spread.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gave a vocabulary for treating jokes and habits as things that compete, mutate and spread.
spotlights.memory_hook: Meme rhymes with gene on purpose: a gene for ideas.

spotlights.name: Shifman's definition of an internet meme
spotlights.spot_it: A group of items with the same template but different content, each made by someone who knew about the others.
spotlights.story_md: The communication scholar **Limor Shifman** of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem gave the most cited definition in her book **Memes in Digital Culture**. An internet meme is not one picture. It is a **group** of digital items that share content, form or stance, that were **created with awareness of each other**, and that are circulated, imitated and transformed by many users. A single viral video is not a meme by this test. It becomes one when people start making their own versions. Her split between viral (spread unchanged) and memetic (spread by changing) is the clearest tool for reading internet culture: watch what people copy, and what they alter.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why remixing, not mere sharing, is the engine of internet culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Viral is a photocopy. A meme is a game of Chinese whispers that everyone joins on purpose.

spotlights.name: Participatory culture
spotlights.spot_it: Fans, users and readers who make things rather than only consume them: fan fiction, remixes, mods, wikis, reaction videos.
spotlights.story_md: The media scholar **Henry Jenkins** studied TV fans long before social media. In **Textual Poachers** (1992) he showed Star Trek fans writing stories, editing videos and running magazines, borrowing the idea of 'poaching' from the French thinker Michel de Certeau. In 2006 he described a **participatory culture**: low barriers to expression, strong support for creating and sharing, informal mentoring where experienced members pass on skills, and members who believe their contributions matter. The internet did not invent this. It removed the cost of printing and posting, so fan habits became everyone's habits. Every comments section, TikTok duet and Wikipedia edit is participatory culture.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shifts the picture from audiences who receive culture to communities that make it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Jenkins saw TikTok in the photocopied fanzines of 1980s Star Trek fans.

spotlights.name: Wikipedia, a culture of rules nobody is paid to enforce
spotlights.when: Launched 15 January 2001; 25 years old on 15 January 2026
spotlights.spot_it: A puzzle globe of jigsaw pieces with letters from many scripts, and talk pages full of shorthand like NPOV and AGF.
spotlights.story_md: Wikipedia is the purest proof that strangers can build a working culture online. It has no editor in chief. Volunteers write and police it, using norms that grew out of early arguments: **neutral point of view**, **verifiability**, **be bold** and **assume good faith**. Disputes are argued on talk pages in a dense in-group vocabulary, from 'citation needed' to 'edit war'. Like every online community it shows extreme participation inequality: most readers never edit, and a small core does most of the work. In January 2026 it turned 25, still run by a nonprofit and still written for free.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows internet culture can produce lasting public goods, not only jokes.
spotlights.memory_hook: Assume good faith: four words that hold up the world's largest encyclopedia.

sections.title: Before the web: the first online tribes
sections.intro_md:
Internet culture is older than the World Wide Web. By the late 1970s and 1980s, a few hundred thousand people, mostly students, programmers and researchers, were already arguing, joking and making friends through text on mainframes and modems.

These early spaces set patterns that still hold. **Usenet** gave us topic groups, the FAQ, flame wars and the word spam as we use it. **Bulletin board systems** and **The WELL** showed that strangers could become a real community, with in-jokes, feuds and funerals. **IRC** invented the chat room and the hashtag-shaped channel name. Hackers kept a dictionary of their slang, the Jargon File, from 1975.

Two things then changed the population. In September 1993, America Online gave its millions of customers access to Usenet, and the old guard felt swamped. And in 1993 CERN put the web's software into the public domain. Culture that had belonged to a few campuses was about to belong to everyone.

spotlights.name: Usenet, the first global discussion network
spotlights.spot_it: Group names like comp.os.minix, rec.arts.sf, alt.folklore.urban: topics separated by dots, read in plain text.
spotlights.story_md: Two Duke University graduate students, **Tom Truscott and Jim Ellis**, conceived Usenet in 1979 so that computers could swap messages over phone lines. Posts were copied from server to server, so no one owned it. Its groups became the first global forums, and much of the internet's vocabulary was born there: FAQ, flame, troll, lurker, spam. History was announced on it too. Tim Berners-Lee posted a summary of the World Wide Web to alt.hypertext on **6 August 1991**, and Linus Torvalds announced a hobby operating system, Linux, on comp.os.minix on **25 August 1991**. The 'alt' hierarchy was set up in 1987 as an escape from the rules about which groups were allowed, an early fight between moderation and freedom.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the template for every forum, subreddit and group chat that followed.
spotlights.memory_hook: The web and Linux were both first announced on Usenet, three weeks apart in 1991.

spotlights.name: The WELL, Sausalito
spotlights.spot_it: A dial-up community run from a houseboat-and-hippie town near San Francisco, with the rule 'You own your own words'.
spotlights.story_md: The **Whole Earth 'Lectronic Link** was started in 1985 by Stewart Brand, editor of the Whole Earth Catalog, and Larry Brilliant, a doctor who had worked on smallpox eradication in India. Users paid by the hour to dial in. Its rule, **You Own Your Own Words**, made each person responsible for what they posted. Grateful Dead fans were among its liveliest early groups. Members held real-world picnics, raised money for sick members and mourned deaths together. The writer Howard Rheingold drew on it for **The Virtual Community** (1993), the book that popularised the term. Brand's slogan from a 1984 hackers' conference, that information wants to be free, became a founding belief of internet culture.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved that online relationships could be as real as offline ones, years before social media.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first online community was run by hippies who paid by the hour.

spotlights.name: IRC and the first chat server
spotlights.spot_it: Channel names that begin with #, nicknames, and lines of text scrolling past in real time.
spotlights.story_md: In August 1988 **Jarkko Oikarinen**, a student working at the University of Oulu in Finland, wrote Internet Relay Chat to replace a clunky messaging program. The first server was a Sun-3 machine called **tolsun.oulu.fi**, which is now on display at the university. IRC gave the world chat rooms named with a #, operators with powers to kick and ban, bots, and a culture of fast, terse banter. It also proved its worth in news: during the 1991 Gulf War and the Soviet coup attempt that August, people relayed reports live on IRC. The # in front of channel names is the direct ancestor of the hashtag.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Real-time group chat, from Slack to Discord, descends from it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every hashtag carries the ghost of a Finnish chat room.

spotlights.name: The September that never ended
spotlights.spot_it: Old-timers complaining that newcomers do not know the rules; the phrase 'Eternal September'.
spotlights.story_md: Every September, US universities gave new students internet access, and Usenet groups filled with freshmen who did not know the etiquette. By October they had learned or left. In **September 1993**, America Online began giving its customers access to Usenet. The newcomers kept coming, and never stopped. In 1994 a Usenet user, Dave Fischer, wrote that September 1993 would go down in net history as the September that never ended. The phrase stuck because it names a pattern every online community lives through: a small group builds norms, it grows, and newcomers arrive faster than the culture can absorb them. Reddit, Twitter and Mastodon have all had their own eternal Septembers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It describes the central tension of online culture: openness versus keeping the norms that made a place good.
spotlights.memory_hook: On the internet it has been September since 1993.

spotlights.name: The web's first server
spotlights.spot_it: A black NeXT cube at CERN with a hand-written label telling people not to switch it off.
spotlights.story_md: Tim Berners-Lee proposed an information system for CERN in March 1989; his boss called it 'vague but exciting'. By the end of 1990 he had the first web server and browser running on a **NeXT computer**, with a label warning colleagues not to power it down. On **30 April 1993** CERN put the web's software in the public domain, and that decision is why anyone could build a website without paying a licence. Graphical browsers followed, and the text-only culture of Usenet and IRC gained pictures, home pages, guestbooks and, soon, animated GIFs. Berners-Lee was knighted in 2004 and has spent decades arguing that the web should stay open.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Giving the web away is what allowed a mass culture, not a corporate one, to grow on it.
spotlights.memory_hook: The machine that started the web had a sticky note begging people not to switch it off.

sections.title: Unwritten rules: netiquette, lurkers and trolls
sections.intro_md:
Every culture has manners, and online ones formed fast because mistakes were public and permanent. Typing in capitals came to mean **shouting**. Asking a question answered in the FAQ earned a curt 'RTFM'. Reposting old content became a minor sin with its own name, the **repost**.

Most of these rules were never voted on. They were taught by correction: a newcomer broke a rule, regulars mocked or explained, and the norm hardened. Some were later written down, as in the 1995 Netiquette guidelines, but the writing came after the habit.

Two roles appear in almost every community. The **lurker** reads without posting, and is by far the majority. The **troll** posts to provoke, and is a minority with outsized effect. Between them sits a third problem with no fix: online, irony and sincerity look identical. A culture that runs on jokes must keep guessing who is joking.

spotlights.name: RFC 1855: the Netiquette guidelines
spotlights.spot_it: A plain text document numbered RFC 1855, with advice like 'Use mixed case. UPPER CASE LOOKS AS IF YOU'RE SHOUTING.'
spotlights.story_md: Internet standards are published as numbered 'Requests for Comments'. In October 1995 **Sally Hambridge** of Intel wrote one that was not about protocols but about people. RFC 1855 told newcomers to lurk before posting, to keep signatures short, to avoid sending angry replies before sleeping on them, and to remember that a reader cannot see your face. It warned that capital letters read as shouting. Many of its rules came straight from a decade of Usenet arguments, and some read like advice for social media in 2026: assume a message may be forwarded, and remember the person on the other end is human.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the moment internet culture wrote down its own manners.
spotlights.memory_hook: Netiquette was published as an internet standard, numbered like a technical protocol.

spotlights.name: The 90-9-1 rule of participation
spotlights.spot_it: A forum with thousands of members where the same twenty names write almost every post.
spotlights.story_md: In October 2006 the usability expert **Jakob Nielsen** described 'participation inequality': in most online communities, about **90%** of users read but never contribute, **9%** contribute now and then, and **1%** create most of the content. The exact numbers vary by site, but the shape holds almost everywhere, from Wikipedia to product reviews. It matters for culture because the 1% set the tone, the slang and the norms that the 90% absorb. What looks like 'what the internet thinks' is usually what a small, very active minority posts. Lurkers are not passive, though. They learn the culture by watching, which is why old communities told newcomers to lurk first.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It warns that online opinion is shaped by a vocal few, not a representative crowd.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ninety watch, nine chip in, one writes the script.

spotlights.name: Trolls, flame wars and Poe's law
spotlights.spot_it: A post that seems too extreme to be real, followed by a hundred furious replies, followed by someone asking 'is this satire?'
spotlights.story_md: **Flaming** was the Usenet word for hostile posting, and a long exchange of it was a flame war. **Trolling** came from a fishing method, dragging bait behind a boat, and by the early 1990s meant posting bait to catch angry replies. In August 2005 a user called Nathan Poe, on a Christian forum, summed up the matching problem: without a wink or obvious sign, a parody of extreme views is impossible to tell from the real thing. **Poe's law** explains much of the internet's confusion. Sincere people are taken for jokers and jokers are taken as sincere, and some extremists hide behind 'it was only a joke'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Knowing that tone cannot be read online is the first step to not being baited.
spotlights.memory_hook: Trolls fish for anger; Poe's law says you cannot tell which bait is real.

sections.title: How a culture forms: the engine room
sections.intro_md:
Strip away the platforms and internet culture forms through a few repeating forces.

**Shared context.** A joke only works for people who know the reference, so in-jokes draw a border around a group. Understanding them is a badge of membership.

**Templates.** The easiest culture to join is one with a fill-in-the-blank format: a picture with top and bottom text, a sound you can dance to, a sentence pattern. Templates turn audiences into authors.

**Affordances.** The design of a platform shapes what grows on it. Character limits produce terse wit; upvotes reward the crowd-pleaser; anonymity frees both honesty and cruelty.

**Emotion and speed.** Content that provokes awe, anger or anxiety is shared more. Studies of Twitter found falsehood and moral outrage travel faster than calm truth.

**Recording.** Everything is archived and searchable, so culture can be studied, revived and, unlike a joke in a pub, held against you years later.

spotlights.name: The image macro and the Impact font
spotlights.spot_it: Thick white capital letters with a black outline across the top and bottom of a photo.
spotlights.story_md: The classic meme format, a picture with a caption above and below, is called an **image macro**. Its typeface, **Impact**, was designed by Geoff Lee in 1965 for the British foundry Stephenson Blake. It became the meme font for a practical reason: Microsoft included it in its free 'core fonts for the web' in the late 1990s, so nearly every computer had it, and its heavy letters stay readable over any photo when given a black outline. Free meme generators then made the format a fill-in-the-blank. Around 2016 to 2018, younger users began to treat Impact captions as old-fashioned, and the plain caption above a picture took over.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a technical accident, a font that came free with Windows, became a visual language.
spotlights.memory_hook: The meme font is a 1965 British typeface that Microsoft gave away.

spotlights.name: The hashtag
spotlights.spot_it: A # in front of a word or phrase, used to join a conversation: #MeToo, #IPL2026, #ThrowbackThursday.
spotlights.story_md: Twitter did not invent the hashtag. On **23 August 2007** a designer named **Chris Messina** tweeted: 'how do you feel about using # (pound) for groups. As in #barcamp?' He borrowed the idea from IRC channel names. Twitter staff reportedly thought it was too nerdy to catch on. Users disagreed: during the San Diego wildfires that October, #sandiegofire helped people follow updates. Twitter made hashtags clickable in 2009. The American Dialect Society named hashtag its Word of the Year for 2012. The retweet and the @reply also began as user habits that the company later built in, a pattern repeated across platforms.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest case of users inventing a feature and the company following.
spotlights.memory_hook: The hashtag was a user's suggestion that Twitter thought was too nerdy.

spotlights.name: Why anger and falsehood travel faster
spotlights.spot_it: A furious post with 50,000 shares beside a calm correction with 50.
spotlights.story_md: Three studies explain why online culture often runs hot. In 2012 **Jonah Berger and Katherine Milkman** analysed about 7,000 New York Times articles and found that content stirring high-arousal emotions, such as awe, anger and anxiety, was more likely to be emailed, while sad content was not. In 2017 **William Brady** and colleagues found that each moral-emotional word in a tweet about politics raised its retweet rate by about **20%**. In 2018 **Soroush Vosoughi, Deb Roy and Sinan Aral** at MIT studied about 126,000 rumour cascades on Twitter from 2006 to 2017. False news was about **70% more likely** to be retweeted, and true stories took about **six times** as long to reach 1,500 people. Bots spread both equally. Humans made the difference.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why rage bait works, and why a culture tuned for sharing tilts towards outrage.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lie gets retweeted 70% more, and truth takes six times as long to arrive.

sections.title: A new way of writing
sections.intro_md:
Online, people write the way they talk, and they had to invent ways to carry tone, timing and tone of voice in text. Linguists such as Gretchen McCulloch, in **Because Internet** (2019), argue this is not decay but a new informal register, as rich as speech.

The tools are familiar. Emoticons and emoji add a face. Lowercase sounds relaxed; a full stop at the end of a short reply can sound cold. Repeated letters stretch a word the way a voice would (soooo). Acronyms like lol began as literal descriptions and became softeners, closer to a polite chuckle than to laughing out loud.

Each language and script built its own version, which is why laughter alone is typed a dozen ways around the world. And some coinages travel far beyond the screen: in 2015 Oxford Dictionaries chose a pictograph, not a word, as its Word of the Year.

spotlights.name: Emoticons and Japanese kaomoji
spotlights.spot_it: Western faces lie sideways :-) while Japanese ones stand upright (^_^) and put the emotion in the eyes.
spotlights.story_md: After Fahlman's smiley, emoticons multiplied in the West, all read by tilting your head: ;-) for a wink, :-P for a tongue. In Japan, users of networks such as ASCII NET in the mid 1980s built faces the right way up, called **kaomoji** (face characters). They focus on the eyes, not the mouth: (^_^) is happy, (T_T) is crying, and (╯°□°)╯︵ ┻━┻ is someone flipping a table in rage. Some psychologists have linked this to culture: studies in Japan and the United States suggested that Japanese readers look to the eyes for emotion, Americans to the mouth. Kaomoji show that even a typed smile is shaped by local habits.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The same need, showing tone, produced different solutions in different cultures.
spotlights.memory_hook: The West smiles with the mouth :-) and Japan with the eyes ^_^.

spotlights.name: Emoji and the Face with Tears of Joy
spotlights.spot_it: A yellow face laughing so hard that two blue tears fly from its eyes.
spotlights.story_md: In 1999 **Shigetaka Kurita**, working on NTT Docomo's i-mode mobile internet in Japan, designed **176 emoji** on a 12 by 12 pixel grid: weather, hearts, faces, a phone. The word comes from Japanese e (picture) and moji (character), not from 'emotion'. In 2010 emoji entered the Unicode standard, and Apple's global emoji keyboard in 2011 took them worldwide. The **Museum of Modern Art** in New York added Kurita's originals to its collection in 2016. In 2015 Oxford Dictionaries named the **Face with Tears of Joy** its Word of the Year, because it was the most used emoji that year in the UK and US. By the 2020s younger users had moved on to the skull emoji, which means 'I'm dead (from laughing)'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Emoji gave the whole world a shared set of faces and symbols, standardised like an alphabet.
spotlights.memory_hook: The word of the year in 2015 was not a word.

spotlights.name: How the world types laughter
spotlights.spot_it: lol in English, 555 in Thai, kkkk in Brazil, jajaja in Spanish, www in Japanese, 233 in China, mdr in France.
spotlights.story_md: Laughter is the most translated sound online. **LOL** appears in a FidoNet newsletter in 1989, and its earlier history is disputed. Thai users type **555**, because five is pronounced 'ha'. Korean users type **ㅋㅋㅋ**, a letter sounding like k. Brazilians write **kkkkk** or **rsrsrs** (from risos, laughs). Spanish speakers write jajaja. Japanese users type **www**, from warau, to laugh, and a long string resembles grass, so laughter is also called kusa, grass. Chinese users write 哈哈 or **233**, the code for a laughing emoticon on the Mop forum. French users write **mdr**, mort de rire, dying of laughter. Hindi speakers, mostly typing in Roman script, write haha, lol and 'hasi aa gayi'.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how each script and language bends the same idea to its own sounds.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Bangkok, a big laugh is 55555.

sections.title: Landmarks: the memes everyone remembers
sections.intro_md:
Internet culture keeps its history in artefacts, and a few became landmarks that almost every regular user of the 2000s and 2010s can still name. They show the full life cycle of a meme: a niche origin, a template that invites copying, a jump to the mainstream, a brand or celebrity cashing in, and finally nostalgia.

They also show how much of this culture is built from ordinary lives. A family video, a pet photo, a pop song nobody had thought about for twenty years and a charity stunt each became global reference points because millions of people chose to copy and change them.

Money arrived late but in force. In 2021, during the NFT boom, the owners of several famous memes sold digital tokens of the originals for sums from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars, a strange receipt for culture that had been made free and shared by everyone.

spotlights.name: Lolcats and I Can Has Cheezburger
spotlights.spot_it: A cat photo with a caption in deliberately broken baby talk: 'I can has cheezburger?'
spotlights.story_md: On 4chan, Saturdays became **Caturday**, when users posted cat pictures with captions. In January 2007 Eric Nakagawa and Kari Unebasami put one, a smiling grey British shorthair asking 'I can has cheezburger?', on a new blog. The site exploded, and later that year it was bought by a group led by **Ben Huh** for a reported 2 million dollars, becoming the base of a network of humour sites. The captions used a made-up dialect, **lolspeak**, with its own grammar. Fans even translated the whole Bible into it. Lolcats were many people's first experience of a meme template: a fixed format into which anyone could drop their own cat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned a 4chan in-joke into one of the first meme businesses.
spotlights.memory_hook: I can has cheezburger? was worth two million dollars.

spotlights.name: The Rickroll
spotlights.spot_it: A link that promises something interesting and plays a man in a trench coat singing 'Never Gonna Give You Up' (1987).
spotlights.story_md: The prank began on 4chan as the **duckroll**, a bait link leading to a picture of a duck on wheels. In May 2007 someone swapped in Rick Astley's 1987 hit, posting a fake link to a Grand Theft Auto IV trailer. On 1 April 2008 YouTube rickrolled its own front page, making every featured video lead to the song. That November, Astley himself appeared on a float in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York and rickrolled a live television audience. The official video passed **1 billion views** on YouTube in July 2021. Astley, who had left pop music in his twenties, gained a new career on the back of a joke at his expense, and he has embraced it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the longest-lived bait-and-switch in internet history, still working nearly two decades later.
spotlights.memory_hook: Never gonna give you up, never gonna let a link be trusted again.

spotlights.name: Gangnam Style breaks the counter
spotlights.spot_it: A man in sunglasses and a tuxedo doing an invisible horse-riding dance, crossed wrists bouncing.
spotlights.story_md: Korean rapper **Psy** released 'Gangnam Style' on 15 July 2012, a satire of the flashy Gangnam district of Seoul. Its horse dance was easy to copy, so parodies poured in from schools, offices and even prisons. On **21 December 2012** it became the first YouTube video to reach **1 billion views**. In December 2014 it went past 2,147,483,647 views, the largest number a 32-bit signed integer can hold, and YouTube said it had upgraded its view counter to a 64-bit number. The song showed that a hit could now travel from Seoul to the world through imitation videos, without radio or a US label.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved a non-English song could become global through participation alone, paving a road for K-pop.
spotlights.memory_hook: One horse dance overflowed YouTube's counter.

spotlights.name: Grumpy Cat
spotlights.spot_it: A small cat with a permanent downturned mouth and a glare, often captioned with a single 'No.'
spotlights.story_md: Her name was **Tardar Sauce**, a mixed-breed cat from Arizona whose frown came from feline dwarfism and an underbite. Her owner's brother, Bryan Bundesen, posted photos on Reddit in **September 2012**, and the internet gave her a personality: a cynic who hated everything. She appeared at festivals, on magazine covers, in a Christmas film and in a waxwork. In 2018 her owners won **710,001 dollars** in a copyright case against a beverage company that had overstepped its licence. She died in May 2019. Grumpy Cat showed a meme could become a brand, with merchandise, agents and lawyers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She marked the moment memes turned into licensed intellectual property.
spotlights.memory_hook: The internet's most famous cynic was a cat who looked grumpy by accident.

spotlights.name: Doge and Kabosu
spotlights.spot_it: A Shiba Inu glancing sideways, surrounded by multicoloured Comic Sans phrases like 'such wow' and 'very meme'.
spotlights.story_md: **Kabosu** was a Shiba Inu adopted in 2008 by Atsuko Sato, a kindergarten teacher in Sakura, Japan. A photo Sato posted on her blog in February 2010 became, in 2013, **Doge**: the dog's side-eye surrounded by broken-English thoughts in Comic Sans. That December, two software engineers launched **Dogecoin** as a joke cryptocurrency with her face on it, and it went on to be worth billions. In June 2021 an NFT of the original photo sold for about **4 million dollars**, with proceeds partly given to charity. Kabosu died on **24 May 2024**, aged 18, and fans around the world mourned a dog most had only ever seen in one sideways glance.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A pet photo became the face of a cryptocurrency and one of the most valuable images on the internet.
spotlights.memory_hook: Such dog, very famous, much Comic Sans.

spotlights.name: The Ice Bucket Challenge
spotlights.spot_it: Someone tipping a bucket of iced water over their own head on camera, then naming three friends to do the same.
spotlights.story_md: In summer 2014, a challenge spread by sportspeople and people living with ALS, including Pete Frates and Pat Quinn, asked people to film themselves being drenched in ice water, donate to ALS research, and nominate others. It was a perfect meme: a simple template, a short deadline, a social obligation and a good cause. About **17 million** people posted videos, from presidents to schoolchildren. The ALS Association reported raising about **115 million dollars** in eight weeks. Critics called it slacktivism, but the money funded real research, including a 2016 study that identified a gene, NEK1, linked to the disease.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that a meme template could move money and science, not just attention.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bucket of ice water found a gene.

sections.title: Platforms are the climate
sections.intro_md:
If memes are the plants of internet culture, platforms are the climate. The same people behave differently on different sites because the design rewards different things.

**Anonymous, ephemeral** boards such as 4chan, where threads vanish and nobody has a name, produce fast, transgressive, often offensive humour and few lasting reputations. **Voting** sites like Reddit reward whatever the crowd agrees on and split into thousands of sub-cultures, each with moderators and rules. **Follower** networks like Twitter reward the quotable and the combative. **Video** sites made faces and voices central, and **algorithmic feeds** like TikTok's 'For You' page broke the link between how many followers you have and how many people see you: a stranger's first video can reach millions.

The founders rarely planned the cultures that grew. Many signature features, from the retweet to the duet, began as users bending a product to their own purposes.

spotlights.name: Me at the zoo: YouTube's first video
spotlights.spot_it: A young man in front of elephants at San Diego Zoo, talking for 19 seconds about their 'really, really, really long trunks'.
spotlights.story_md: YouTube was founded in 2005 by three former PayPal employees, Chad Hurley, Steve Chen and **Jawed Karim**. Karim, born in Germany to a Bangladeshi father, uploaded the first video on **23 April 2005**: 19 seconds at San Diego Zoo, filmed by a school friend. It has no edit, no music and no point, and that is its charm. It shows what YouTube's culture would value at first: the unpolished, the personal, the 'broadcast yourself' of its early slogan. Within two years ordinary people were famous for webcam confessions and home videos, and the vlogger was born. Today the video has hundreds of millions of views and is a pilgrimage site in the comments.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It set the tone for a platform that made everyday people into broadcasters.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first YouTube video is 19 seconds about elephant trunks.

spotlights.name: 4chan and the anonymous culture
spotlights.spot_it: A plain pale page of image threads, posters all named 'Anonymous', and boards with letters like /b/.
spotlights.story_md: **Christopher Poole**, a 15-year-old in New York using the name moot, started 4chan in October 2003 as an English copy of Japan's Futaba Channel image board. Posting is anonymous by default and old threads are deleted, so nothing has an author and nothing lasts. That mix produced a large share of early meme culture: lolcats, the Rickroll, rage comics and the protest group **Anonymous**, which first marched against the Church of Scientology in 2008. It also bred harassment campaigns, hoaxes and extremist spaces, and its boards were linked to several mass shooters' posts. In 2015 Poole sold the site to Hiroyuki Nishimura, founder of Japan's 2channel.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how anonymity and impermanence create creativity and cruelty from the same soil.
spotlights.memory_hook: On 4chan everyone is Anonymous, so the culture belongs to no one.

spotlights.name: Reddit, the front page of the internet
spotlights.spot_it: An orange-red alien mascot, up and down arrows beside every post, and thousands of communities starting with r/.
spotlights.story_md: **Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian**, roommates at the University of Virginia, founded Reddit in 2005 in the first batch of the startup school Y Combinator. To make the empty site look busy, they posted under many fake accounts. Voting decides what rises, so the crowd sets the taste. From 2008 users could create **subreddits**, and these became cultures with their own rules and slang. In April 2017 an experiment called **r/place** let users each place one pixel every few minutes on a shared canvas, and rival communities fought and allied for 72 hours, a model of internet culture in miniature. In June 2023 thousands of subreddits went dark in protest at new fees for outside apps.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed how voting and volunteer moderators can make thousands of self-governing subcultures.
spotlights.memory_hook: Reddit faked its first crowd so a real one would come.

compare.difference: Reddit has persistent usernames, karma and votes; 4chan is anonymous and threads disappear.

spotlights.name: Twitter and the 140-character voice
spotlights.spot_it: Short public posts, @names, retweets and hashtags; renamed X in 2023.
spotlights.story_md: Twitter grew from a side project at a podcast company. Jack Dorsey sent the first tweet on 21 March 2006: 'just setting up my twttr'. Its limit of **140 characters** came from the 160-character text message, leaving room for a username. The constraint created a style: compressed jokes, punchlines, quote-tweets and pile-ons. Users invented its grammar, from the @reply to RT and the hashtag. Twitter became the place where journalists, politicians and comedians performed in public, and so the home of the 'main character of the day'. The limit doubled to 280 in November 2017. After Elon Musk bought it in 2022, it was renamed X in July 2023.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Its constraints shaped how a generation writes jokes and arguments online.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twitter's limit came from SMS: 160 characters minus 20 for your name.

spotlights.name: Vine, TikTok and the algorithmic feed
spotlights.spot_it: Vertical full-screen video, a sound you have heard a hundred times, and a feed that knows you better than your friends.
spotlights.story_md: **Vine**, launched by Twitter in January 2013, limited videos to **six seconds** and looped them, and comedians learned to land a joke in that time. It shut in January 2017, but its creators and timing moved on. ByteDance launched **Douyin** in China in 2016 and **TikTok** abroad in 2017, merging it with Musical.ly in 2018. TikTok's key idea was the 'For You' page, which shows videos based on what you watch, not who you follow. Culture now forms around **sounds**: a clip of audio becomes a template that thousands reuse for dances, jokes and stories. Duets and stitches let users reply in video. Trends can rise and die within a week.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The algorithmic feed made anyone a potential star and sped the life cycle of memes to days.
spotlights.memory_hook: Vine gave you six seconds; TikTok gave the algorithm your attention.

sections.title: Fans who build worlds
sections.intro_md:
Fans were the internet's first heavy users and remain its most organised. Long before brands discovered 'community', fans ran mailing lists, archives, wikis, translation teams and voting drives.

Fan culture has its own norms: tagging content carefully, crediting creators, warning about spoilers, and a gift economy where stories, art and videos are given away. It also has its own conflicts, between fans and creators, between rival fan groups, and inside fandoms over who gets to interpret a story.

The scale is enormous. Archive of Our Own, a volunteer-built fan fiction site, held more than **18 million works** across about 83,000 fandoms by September 2026. K-pop fan groups coordinate streaming goals, trend hashtags and charity drives across continents. And the word for a devoted fan, **stan**, comes from a dark rap song about an obsessive one.

spotlights.name: Archive of Our Own
spotlights.when: Founded 2008; open beta November 2009; left beta April 2026
spotlights.spot_it: A plain red-and-white site of stories with long tag lists: fandom, characters, relationships, warnings.
spotlights.story_md: In 2007 the novelist **Naomi Novik** called for fans to build 'an archive of one's own', echoing Virginia Woolf, so their work would not depend on companies that might delete it. The nonprofit **Organization for Transformative Works** built AO3 with volunteer coders, mostly women, many of whom learned to program on the project. Volunteer **tag wranglers** link millions of user-written tags so readers can find anything. In 2019 AO3 won a **Hugo Award**, science fiction's top prize, for Best Related Work. It finally dropped its 'beta' label on **2 April 2026**, more than 16 years after opening. By September 2026 it held about 18.47 million works.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the largest proof that a fan gift economy can build and run major infrastructure.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Hugo went to an archive built and tagged by unpaid fans.

spotlights.name: Stan: from a song to a verb
spotlights.when: Song 2000; in the Oxford English Dictionary 2019
spotlights.spot_it: 'I stan', or an account called 'stan account' devoted entirely to one singer, actor or team.
spotlights.story_md: In 2000 Eminem released **'Stan'**, a song in the form of letters from an obsessive fan who ends in tragedy. Online, the name became a word for an extremely devoted fan, first as a mild insult, then as a badge. Fans began to say 'I stan' as a verb. The Oxford English Dictionary added both noun and verb in **2019**. Stan culture brought coordinated tactics: mass streaming to push songs up charts, flooding hashtags, and sometimes harassing critics. K-pop fandoms such as BTS's ARMY raised large sums for causes, and in June 2020 K-pop fans flooded a police app and a racist hashtag with fancams, showing fandom tactics can be pointed at politics.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how fan devotion became an organised, sometimes political force online.
spotlights.memory_hook: A song about a dangerous fan became the word fans proudly use for themselves.

sections.title: When it turns: harm, backfire and lost context
sections.intro_md:
The same forces that make internet culture inventive make it dangerous. Copying, recording and speed do not care whether the subject agreed.

Some harms come from **mobs**. A post, a video or a single bad joke can make a private person the target of millions, a pattern sometimes called public shaming or pile-ons. Some come from **context collapse**: a remark meant for friends is read by strangers with no idea of the joke. Some come from **coordinated trolling**, where groups organise raids or teach machines to misbehave. Others come from the **attention economy** itself, which pays for outrage.

There is also a strange law of backfire. Trying to delete something online often makes it spread further, because the attempt itself becomes news.

None of this is unique to the internet, but scale is new. A playground teasing used to stay in the playground.

spotlights.name: Star Wars Kid
spotlights.spot_it: A teenager swinging a golf ball retriever like a lightsaber in an empty school studio.
spotlights.story_md: In November 2002 **Ghyslain Raza**, a 14-year-old in Trois-Rivières, Quebec, filmed himself swinging a golf ball retriever like a Jedi weapon. He left the tape at school. Classmates found it and uploaded it in April 2003. It became one of the first viral videos, remixed with lightsaber effects and watched by millions. For Raza it was a nightmare: he was mocked in school and online, left school and received psychiatric care. His family sued the classmates' families and settled in 2006. In 2013, as an adult who had become a lawyer, he spoke publicly for the first time about the harm and urged people to show empathy.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was an early warning that viral fame can be cruelty at scale, especially for children.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first viral video star never chose to be one.

spotlights.name: The Streisand effect
spotlights.spot_it: Any time a takedown, lawsuit or ban makes the thing it targets far more famous.
spotlights.story_md: In 2003 the photographer Kenneth Adelman was documenting coastal erosion in California for a public archive of about 12,000 aerial photos. One, Image 3850, showed **Barbra Streisand's** clifftop house in Malibu. She sued for 50 million dollars to have it removed. Before the lawsuit, the image had been downloaded **six times**, two of them by her own lawyers. After news of the suit spread, about **420,000 people** visited the page within a month. She lost the case. In 2005 Mike Masnick of Techdirt named the pattern the **Streisand effect**. It is now a basic law of internet culture: attempts at suppression become content.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why censorship and takedowns often backfire online.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six downloads before the lawsuit, 420,000 visits after.

spotlights.name: Tay, the chatbot that learned too well
spotlights.spot_it: A cheerful Twitter bot with a teenage girl persona that turned offensive within hours.
spotlights.story_md: On **23 March 2016** Microsoft launched **Tay**, an AI chatbot on Twitter designed to talk like an American teenager and learn from conversations. Users, some organised on 4chan and 8chan, flooded it with racist and inflammatory messages, and Tay began repeating them. It sent about 96,000 tweets before Microsoft took it offline about **16 hours** after launch, and apologised. Tay became a parable for the AI era: a system that learns from internet culture absorbs its worst corners too, especially when trolls treat it as a game. Its lessons were cited again when generative AI chatbots arrived in 2022 and 2023.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that internet culture can be weaponised to train machines, not only people.
spotlights.memory_hook: Microsoft's teenage bot lasted 16 hours on Twitter.

spotlights.name: Context collapse
spotlights.spot_it: A joke written for friends, screenshotted and shared to strangers who read it at face value.
spotlights.story_md: Offline, people adjust what they say to the room: friends, family, boss. Online, those audiences collapse into one. The researchers **Alice Marwick and danah boyd** described this **context collapse** in a 2011 study of Twitter users, who coped by imagining an audience and writing for it. The trouble comes when the post escapes. A dark joke for twelve followers is seen by twelve million, with none of the shared context that made it funny. Screenshots and quote posts accelerate it. Much of the internet's shaming, cancellation and misunderstanding can be traced to collapse: words travel, but the room they were spoken in does not.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why online speech is riskier than speech in a room, even when it feels private.
spotlights.memory_hook: Online, every room is the same room.

sections.title: One internet, many cultures
sections.intro_md:
It is easy to imagine internet culture as American, because so many global platforms and memes started in the United States. But each country and language built its own, shaped by its script, its politics, its platforms and its humour.

Japan had its own anonymous boards before 4chan, and 4chan was copied from them. China, behind its firewall, grew a parallel universe of apps and a sophisticated language of puns to discuss what censors would delete. South Korea built a gaming culture around PC bangs, internet cafes open all night, and later exported K-pop through fan participation. Brazil and India made a Google social network, Orkut, their own, long after Americans had left it.

The same forces appear everywhere: in-jokes, templates, platforms and speed. The results are different, and the differences say a lot about each place.

spotlights.name: The Grass Mud Horse
spotlights.spot_it: An alpaca, plush toy or cartoon, with the Chinese characters 草泥马 and a reference to 'river crabs'.
spotlights.story_md: In early 2009 Chinese users invented a mythical animal, the **cǎo ní mǎ**, or grass mud horse, said to live in a desert whose name, like the animal's, sounds almost exactly like a vulgar insult. Its enemy was the **river crab**, héxiè, which sounds like the word for 'harmony', the official reason given for censorship. So being 'harmonised' meant being censored. The animal was pictured as an alpaca, and alpaca toys sold out. Because the words were technically about animals, filters could not easily block them. It is a perfect example of an internet culture forming as resistance: a shared code that says something the authorities cannot easily delete.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how wordplay lets online communities talk around censorship.
spotlights.memory_hook: In China, an alpaca became a protest against censors.

spotlights.name: Danmaku: comments that fly across the video
spotlights.spot_it: Hundreds of lines of text scrolling across a video, timed to the moment each viewer typed them.
spotlights.story_md: In December 2006 the Japanese site **Niconico Douga** let viewers type comments that fly across the screen at the exact second of the video they refer to. The effect, called **danmaku** (bullet curtain), turns solitary viewing into a crowd watching together, even when the comments were typed months apart. China's **Bilibili**, founded in 2009 for anime fans, made danmaku central and grew into one of China's major video platforms. Viewers shout 'front row', count down, and fill the screen with text at the climax of a scene. It is a different answer to the same question every platform faces: how to make watching feel social.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a design choice can create a whole etiquette of shared viewing.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Japan and China, the comments section lives inside the video.

spotlights.name: 2channel, Japan's anonymous giant
spotlights.spot_it: Endless threads of anonymous text posts, elaborate ASCII art, and a story called 'Train Man'.
spotlights.story_md: **Hiroyuki Nishimura**, then a university student, launched **2channel** in 1999. Everyone posted anonymously, and it grew into one of the largest forums on earth, a home for gossip, politics, otaku culture and elaborate ASCII art. In 2004 a series of posts in which an anonymous user asked for dating advice after defending a woman on a train became **Densha Otoko** (Train Man), turned into a bestselling book, a film and a TV drama. 2channel inspired Futaba Channel, which inspired 4chan. In a neat loop, Nishimura bought 4chan in 2015. After a dispute over control in 2014, the original site was later renamed 5channel.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the ancestor of the anonymous image-board culture that shaped Western memes.
spotlights.memory_hook: The man who built Japan's 2channel ended up owning 4chan.

spotlights.name: Orkut, Brazil's and India's first social network
spotlights.spot_it: A blue and pink site with 'scraps' on your profile, testimonials from friends, and communities for everything.
spotlights.story_md: Google engineer **Orkut Büyükkökten** built a social network in 2004 and named it after himself. Americans drifted away, but **Brazilians** made it theirs, and they were for years the large majority of its users. **India** became its second big market, and for millions of Indians in the late 2000s it was the first social network: scrapbooks, fake celebrity profiles, college communities and fan clubs. Brazilian users were so dominant that English-speaking users complained, a reverse Eternal September. Facebook overtook it in both countries by 2010 to 2011, and Google shut Orkut on **30 September 2014**. Many Indians still speak of it with nostalgia.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that a platform's culture is decided by who adopts it, not who builds it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Orkut was American-built, Brazilian-run and Indian-loved.

sections.title: India's internet: from Orkut to Reels
sections.intro_md:
India's internet culture arrived in two waves. The first, in the 2000s, was English-speaking, urban and on desktops: Orkut scraps, college forums, cyber cafes, chain emails and early Bollywood fan sites. The second came on cheap smartphones after **2016**, when Reliance **Jio** launched with free and then very cheap data, and hundreds of millions of people came online for the first time, many in small towns and villages, many in Indian languages.

That second wave changed the culture. It made India **video-first and voice-first**, built on WhatsApp, YouTube, short-video apps and Instagram Reels. It made Hinglish, regional languages and film dialogue the raw material of memes. And it made India's internet culture one of the largest in the world: about 958 million active users in 2025, 57% of them rural, with 588 million watching short videos.

The results range from global hits to real-world harm, from Kolaveri Di to WhatsApp rumours that ended in violence.

spotlights.name: Why This Kolaveri Di
spotlights.spot_it: A man in a recording studio with headphones, singing 'Why this kolaveri kolaveri di' in Tamil-accented English.
spotlights.story_md: The actor **Dhanush** and the 21-year-old composer **Anirudh Ravichander** made the song for the Tamil film '3'. Anirudh composed the tune in about 10 minutes and Dhanush wrote the lyrics in about 20, in **Tanglish**: English words used with Tamil grammar, about a boy dumped by a girl ('kolaveri' means murderous rage). A version leaked, so the studio released the making-of video on **16 November 2011**. It had about 3.5 million views in a week and over 30 million by early 2012, topped Indian Twitter trends, and drew cover versions around the world. The Prime Minister, Manmohan Singh, invited Dhanush as a guest. It was India's first true viral song of the social media age.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved that an Indian-language, unpolished song could go global through sharing alone.
spotlights.memory_hook: A ten-minute tune in broken English became India's first viral anthem.

spotlights.name: The Jio effect
spotlights.spot_it: Families watching YouTube on a single phone; mobile data bought in daily packs of 1.5 GB.
spotlights.story_md: Reliance Jio launched commercially on **5 September 2016** with free data and calls until March 2017. It signed up about 16 million subscribers in its first month and passed 100 million by February 2017. Rivals cut prices to survive, and mobile data in India went from among the world's more expensive to among its cheapest within a few years. The cultural effect was enormous. Hundreds of millions of first-time users came online through phones, often skipping email and the desktop web entirely. Video replaced text, voice search replaced typing, and Indian language content, devotional videos, rural comedy and regional film clips found audiences larger than many countries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned India's internet culture from an urban English niche into a mass culture in many languages.
spotlights.memory_hook: Jio made data cheaper than tea, and India went online on video.

spotlights.name: WhatsApp forwards and good morning images
spotlights.spot_it: A sunrise, a flower or a deity with 'Good Morning' in glittering letters, and a message labelled 'Forwarded many times'.
spotlights.story_md: For many Indian families, **WhatsApp** is the internet. Its culture includes the daily **good morning** image, so common that in January 2018 the Wall Street Journal reported Google researchers finding that one in three Indian smartphone users ran out of storage every day, partly because of them. It also includes the forward: unverified news, cures and rumours passed between groups. In 2017 and 2018, rumours about child kidnappers spread on WhatsApp were followed by mob lynchings in several states, killing dozens of people. In **July 2018** WhatsApp limited forwarding in India to **five chats** at once and later took the rule worldwide, and in 2020 tightened it to one chat for 'highly forwarded' messages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a culture's sharing habits can carry kindness and misinformation in the same channel.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sunrise and a rumour travel in the same family group.

spotlights.name: The TikTok ban and the rise of Reels
spotlights.spot_it: Short vertical videos of village comedy, lip-sync and dance, now on Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts, Moj or Josh.
spotlights.story_md: By 2020 India was TikTok's biggest market by users, with figures of about 200 million commonly reported. Small-town creators, farmers, labourers and homemakers became stars, often performing in Hindi, Bhojpuri, Tamil or Punjabi. On **29 June 2020**, after a deadly border clash with China, the government blocked **59 Chinese apps**, including TikTok, under the IT Act. Within days, Indian apps such as Moj and Josh rushed to fill the gap, and on 8 July 2020 Instagram launched **Reels** in India, one of its first big markets. YouTube Shorts followed. The creators and the culture survived the ban: they simply moved platforms, taking their sounds and formats with them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved that an internet culture lives in its people and formats, not in any one app.
spotlights.memory_hook: TikTok was banned in India; TikTok culture was not.

spotlights.name: Baburao and Bollywood meme templates
spotlights.spot_it: A man in thick glasses, a vest and a dhoti, looking up in despair: 'Utha le re baba'.
spotlights.story_md: India's meme culture runs on film. The richest source is **Hera Pheri** (2000), in which **Paresh Rawal** plays Baburao Ganpatrao Apte, a short-tempered, short-sighted landlord. Lines like 'Utha le re baba' (take me away, God) and 'Ye Baburao ka style hai' became reaction templates used for exams, cricket, politics and office life. Other films supplied a whole grammar: dialogues from Phir Hera Pheri, Welcome, Gangs of Wasseypur and countless Tamil and Telugu comedies. Because Indian audiences already share these films, a still frame carries a whole joke, the same shared-context engine that powered lolcats, built on a cinema that unites a country of many languages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a national cinema became the shared vocabulary for a multilingual internet.
spotlights.memory_hook: In India, the meme library is the film archive.

spotlights.name: Lockdown memes: Rasode mein kaun tha and Binod
spotlights.spot_it: A soap opera matriarch shouting the same line on a beat; a comment section filled with the single word 'Binod'.
spotlights.story_md: In August 2020, with India in lockdown, music producer **Yashraj Mukhate** turned a melodramatic scene from the TV serial Saath Nibhaana Saathiya, in which Kokilaben interrogates her family about an empty cooker, into a song: **'Rasode mein kaun tha?'** (who was in the kitchen?). It went viral and launched a new genre of turning dialogue into music. The same month, a YouTube video by the channel Slayy Point mocked Indian comment sections, singling out a user who had simply typed his own name, **Binod**. Within days 'Binod' filled comment sections, streams and even brand accounts. Both were pure internet culture: meaningless to outsiders, a passport for insiders.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a shared crisis produced a burst of participatory humour in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Binod became famous for typing 'Binod'.

spotlights.name: Pawri ho rahi hai: a meme that crossed the border
spotlights.spot_it: A young woman filming her friends by a car in the mountains: 'Yeh humari car hai, aur yeh hum hain, aur yeh humari pawri ho rahi hai.'
spotlights.story_md: In February 2021 a Pakistani student and influencer, **Dananeer Mobeen**, posted a short clip mocking posh accents: this is our car, this is us, and this is our 'pawri' (party), said in an exaggerated way. Yashraj Mukhate remixed it into a song, and it swept India. Police departments and brands made their own versions. For a few weeks, a joke from Pakistan united timelines on both sides of one of the world's most tense borders, a reminder that internet culture follows language and humour more than national lines.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows memes can cross political borders that people often cannot.
spotlights.memory_hook: One 'pawri' was attended by two countries.

spotlights.name: Moye moye: a Serbian song becomes an Indian sigh
spotlights.spot_it: A sad, dramatic chorus, 'moye moye', played over a clip of something going wrong.
spotlights.story_md: The Serbian singer **Teya Dora** released 'Džanum' in 2023, with a haunting chorus in which 'moje more' means 'my nightmares'. In late 2023 Indian creators began using the line, heard as 'moye moye', as a sound for disappointment and failure: a missed catch, a failed exam, a cancelled plan. Most had no idea what the words meant, which did not matter. The sound became so widespread in India that it pushed the song up streaming charts there, and Teya Dora went on to represent Serbia at Eurovision in 2024. It shows a now typical pattern: a sound travels, loses its original meaning and gains a new one.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how TikTok-style sound culture rewrites the meaning of songs across languages.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Serbian it means 'my nightmares'; in India it means 'oops'.

spotlights.name: India's Got Latent and the limits of edgy humour
spotlights.spot_it: A comedian judging contestants in front of a live audience, clips cut into reels.
spotlights.story_md: **Samay Raina**, a stand-up comic and chess streamer, built **India's Got Latent** as an online talent show with deliberately harsh, crude judging, a format born from internet roast culture. In February 2025 a remark by guest judge Ranveer Allahbadia, a popular podcaster, provoked national outrage. Police complaints were filed in several states, MPs called for action, and the Supreme Court sharply criticised the remark while hearing his plea. Raina deleted the episodes. The episode became a test of where internet humour collides with offline norms and law in India, and of how quickly context collapse can turn an in-group joke into a national controversy.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a recent Indian case of context collapse with legal consequences.
spotlights.memory_hook: A joke for a live room became a case in the Supreme Court.

sections.title: Myths and older-than-you-think
sections.intro_md:
Internet culture likes to believe it invented everything. Much of it is older.

**Myth: memes are a creation of the internet.** Fact: the word dates from 1976, and the behaviour, from graffiti to chain letters to playground rhymes, is ancient. The internet changed the speed and the record, not the instinct.

**Myth: emoticons began in 1982.** Fact: Fahlman's smiley is the first documented use of :-) for tone online, but typographic faces appeared in print in 1881.

**Myth: internet culture is only for the young.** Fact: Indian WhatsApp good morning images, Facebook groups and YouTube devotional channels are run largely by older users. Each generation has its own internet culture.

**Myth: online behaviour is not 'real' life.** Fact: online norms shape jobs, elections, music charts and courts. The Ice Bucket Challenge funded genetics research; WhatsApp rumours ended in deaths.

**Myth: brain rot is a new phrase.** Fact: Henry David Thoreau used it in Walden in 1854, complaining about a taste for simple ideas.

spotlights.name: Kilroy was here
spotlights.spot_it: A bald head with a long nose peeking over a wall, fingers gripping the edge, with the words 'Kilroy was here'.
spotlights.story_md: During the Second World War, American servicemen drew a little face peeping over a wall, with 'Kilroy was here', on walls, ships and bombed buildings across Europe and the Pacific. The most popular origin story points to James J. Kilroy, a shipyard inspector in Quincy, Massachusetts, who chalked the phrase on work he had checked, but nobody is sure. In Britain a similar face was called Mr Chad and came with 'Wot, no ___?' about wartime shortages. The doodle was a meme in every sense Dawkins meant: a simple template, copied by thousands of people who knew about each other, spreading with no central author. It is even hidden in the National WWII Memorial in Washington, opened in 2004.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proves meme culture is human, not digital: the internet only accelerated it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Before the Rickroll, there was Kilroy.

sections.title: What is happening now, 2025 to 2026
sections.intro_md:
Internet culture in 2025 and 2026 is shaped by three forces: **algorithms**, **AI** and **regulation**.

The dictionaries tell the story. Oxford chose **brain rot** for 2024. For 2025 Dictionary.com picked **67** (announced 29 October 2025), Oxford picked **rage bait** (1 December 2025) and Merriam-Webster picked **slop** (15 December 2025), meaning low-quality content mass-produced with AI. All three are words about the internet looking at itself, uneasily.

Governments moved too. Australia's ban on social media accounts for under-16s took effect on **10 December 2025**, and platforms had removed about **4.7 million** accounts by mid-January 2026. In the US, TikTok avoided a ban when a deal creating an American-controlled joint venture closed on **22 January 2026**.

Meanwhile old institutions of internet culture reached milestones: Wikipedia turned 25 on 15 January 2026, and Archive of Our Own left 'beta' on 2 April 2026.

spotlights.name: 67, rage bait and slop: the words of 2025
spotlights.spot_it: Teenagers shouting 'six seven' while weighing their hands up and down; a feed of strange AI videos.
spotlights.story_md: **67**, said 'six seven', is a pure in-joke. It traces to the 2024 drill track 'Doot Doot (6 7)' by Skrilla, then clips linked to basketball player LaMelo Ball, who is 6 feet 7. Its meaning is unclear by design, which is the point: Dictionary.com chose it for 2025 for how fast it spread among children, to teachers' despair. **Rage bait**, Oxford's choice, is content designed to make you angry so you engage; its use tripled in a year, though the phrase dates to at least 2002 on Usenet. **Slop**, Merriam-Webster's choice, names the flood of cheap AI-made content. Together they map 2025: nonsense, anger and machines.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The dictionaries' choices show that internet culture now names its own problems.
spotlights.memory_hook: 2025 in three words: six seven, rage bait, slop.

spotlights.name: Australia's under-16 social media ban
spotlights.spot_it: Teenagers in Australia logged out of Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and YouTube accounts.
spotlights.story_md: Australia passed a law in November 2024 requiring major platforms to take 'reasonable steps' to stop under-16s from holding accounts, with fines of up to **49.5 million Australian dollars**. It took effect on **10 December 2025**, the first such national rule in the world. By mid-January 2026 the eSafety Commissioner, **Julie Inman Grant**, reported that platforms had removed about **4.7 million** accounts. Teenagers reported dodging age checks, sometimes with help from parents, and in 2026 the government moved to tighten enforcement after reports of weak compliance. Other countries are watching. For internet culture, it is a test of whether youth culture can be fenced off from the platforms where it lives.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the first national attempt to remove an entire age group from mainstream social media.

sections.title: Recap: how a culture forms online
sections.intro_md:
Internet culture is the shared language, humour, manners, values and artefacts of people who meet through networks. It forms the way all culture does, through imitation and belonging, but with four accelerants: anyone can publish, anything can be copied and changed, everything travels at once, and everything is recorded.

The story runs from Usenet's newsgroups and Fahlman's smiley in 1982, through The WELL, IRC and the Eternal September of 1993, to image boards, Reddit, YouTube, Twitter and the algorithmic feeds of TikTok and Reels. At each step, the design of the platform shaped the culture: anonymity, votes, character limits, sounds.

The engine is constant. **In-jokes** draw borders. **Templates** turn watchers into makers. **Emotion**, especially outrage, speeds sharing. A small, active minority writes most of it. Trying to suppress something often spreads it. And context collapse turns private jokes into public scandals.

India now holds one of the world's biggest internet cultures, multilingual, video-first and film-fluent. Next time a phrase like 'moye moye' or 'six seven' appears in your feed, ask: who started it, what template does it use, and when will the insiders drop it?

best_facts.fact: Before Barbra Streisand sued to suppress a photo of her house in 2003, it had been downloaded six times, two of them by her lawyers. After the suit, about 420,000 people looked.
best_facts.why_surprising: The lawsuit created the audience it tried to stop.

best_facts.fact: On Twitter, false news was about 70% more likely to be retweeted than true news, and true stories took about six times as long to reach 1,500 people.
best_facts.why_surprising: Bots spread both equally; humans tilted the field.

best_facts.fact: Gangnam Style passed 2,147,483,647 views in 2014, the largest number a 32-bit signed integer can hold, and YouTube moved to a 64-bit counter.
best_facts.why_surprising: A horse dance outgrew the arithmetic of the world's biggest video site.

best_facts.fact: The hashtag was proposed by a user, Chris Messina, in 2007. Twitter's staff reportedly thought it was too nerdy.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the internet's defining symbols came from a customer, not the company.

best_facts.fact: The World Wide Web and Linux were both first announced on Usenet, within three weeks of each other in August 1991.
best_facts.why_surprising: Two foundations of modern computing debuted as forum posts.

best_facts.fact: In 2015 Oxford Dictionaries' Word of the Year was not a word but an emoji: the Face with Tears of Joy.
best_facts.why_surprising: A pictograph beat every English word.

best_facts.fact: Thai internet users type 555 to laugh, because five in Thai is pronounced 'ha'.
best_facts.why_surprising: Laughter can be written in numbers.

best_facts.fact: The founder of Japan's 2channel, Hiroyuki Nishimura, bought 4chan in 2015, the American site that had been copied from a 2channel offshoot.
best_facts.why_surprising: The family tree of anonymous boards folded back on itself.

best_facts.fact: 'Brain rot', Oxford's Word of the Year for 2024, was first used by Henry David Thoreau in Walden in 1854.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most online phrase of 2024 is 170 years old.

best_facts.fact: Microsoft's Tay chatbot lasted about 16 hours on Twitter in March 2016 before trolls taught it to post racist messages.
best_facts.why_surprising: A machine learned internet culture's worst corner in less than a day.

best_facts.fact: The ALS Association raised about 115 million dollars in eight weeks from the 2014 Ice Bucket Challenge, money that helped fund the discovery of a gene linked to the disease.
best_facts.why_surprising: A soaking meme produced real science.

best_facts.fact: In 2009 Chinese users invented the 'grass mud horse', an alpaca whose name sounds like an insult, to mock censors, who were 'river crabs' because hexie sounds like 'harmony'.
best_facts.why_surprising: An alpaca became a symbol of resistance.

best_facts.fact: Reddit's founders posted under many fake accounts in the early days so the site would look busy.
best_facts.why_surprising: The front page of the internet began as a staged crowd.

best_facts.fact: Twitter's 140-character limit came from SMS: 160 characters, minus 20 for a username.
best_facts.why_surprising: A phone standard shaped a generation's style of wit.

best_facts.fact: Fahlman's original 1982 smiley post was lost for 20 years and recovered from old backup tapes in 2002.
best_facts.why_surprising: The birth certificate of online tone nearly vanished.

best_facts.fact: Archive of Our Own, a fan fiction site run by volunteers, won science fiction's Hugo Award in 2019 and only dropped its 'beta' label in April 2026.
best_facts.why_surprising: A prize-winning archive stayed officially unfinished for 16 years.

best_facts.fact: In 2018 Google researchers found that one in three Indian smartphone users ran out of phone storage every day, partly because of 'good morning' images on WhatsApp.
best_facts.why_surprising: Greetings, not videos or games, were filling India's phones.

best_facts.fact: Australia's under-16 social media ban, in force from 10 December 2025, led platforms to remove about 4.7 million accounts in its first month.
best_facts.why_surprising: A whole age group was logged out by law.

side_dish.title: Whales have memes too
side_dish.body_md:
If you think internet culture is the fastest culture on Earth, meet the humpback whale.

Male humpbacks sing long, complex songs during the breeding season, and all males in a population sing roughly the same song. That song is **learned**, not inherited. Every year it changes a little, as whales add, drop and alter phrases, the way slang shifts.

In 2011 the biologist **Ellen Garland** and colleagues published a study in Current Biology tracking songs across the South Pacific over 11 years. They found something remarkable: new song types appeared off eastern **Australia** and then spread **eastward**, population by population, to New Caledonia, Tonga, the Cook Islands and French Polynesia. Within one or two seasons, each population dropped its old song and adopted the new one. Researchers called it **cultural revolution** at an ocean-basin scale.

That is a meme in Dawkins' original sense: a unit of behaviour copied from one individual to another, with variation and selection. The whales even show trend cycles: a novel song sweeps in, everyone sings it, and then it is replaced.

There are differences. Whales do not remix on purpose, and their 'feed' is the ocean, moving at the speed of migration rather than light. But the logic is the same as Rickroll or moye moye. Culture is not uniquely human, and copying is older than the internet by millions of years. The internet just put it on fast-forward.

offline_task.title: Trace one meme in your own life
offline_task.body_md:
Pick one meme, phrase or sound you saw this week: a WhatsApp forward, a Reels audio, a line your friends keep repeating.

**1. Find its origin.** Ask the person who used it where they got it. Then ask the person before them, if you can. Write down the chain. How many steps until nobody knows?

**2. Name its template.** What stays the same each time (the picture, the sound, the sentence shape), and what changes? That fixed part is why it spreads.

**3. Find its border.** Try it on three people: someone younger, someone your age, someone older. Who gets it? Who does not? You have just found the edge of an in-group.

**4. Guess its death date.** Has a brand, a politician or a parent used it yet? If yes, insiders are probably already moving on.

Write your findings in five lines. You have done what researchers like Limor Shifman do: treat a joke as a piece of culture, with an origin, a form and a community.
